reason: The turning sensor cells fit at the base of the fluid-filled loops, where moving fluid bends their hairs.
expectation: The combined loops and cells should detect changes in turning.

alternatives.reason: The pictures also show how to build the separate tilt sensors.

effect: The loops and cells form turning sensors, so I can build the separate tilt sensors next.
reaction: The fluid bending the flap makes the turning signal easier to picture.
reason: The picture places the mineral weights on the jelly above the tilt sensor cells.
expectation: The weights and sensor cells should form tilt sensors that respond when the jelly layer shifts.

effect: The weighted sensors are complete; their shifting layer responds to tilt and changes in straight-line movement.
reaction: The crystals bending the sensor hairs make their role clearer.
reason: The balance nerves are pictured carrying signals from both kinds of sensor to the brain.
expectation: The turning sensors should connect to the balance nerve route.

alternatives.reason: The weighted sensors also need a route to the brain.

effect: The turning and weighted sensors had to be joined into balance organs before connecting their nerves.
reaction: I expected a direct nerve connection, so the required pairing surprised me.
reason: The balance nerves are shown leading from both sensor types toward the brain.
expectation: The balance organs should gain a route for sending signals to the brain.

effect: The balance organs cannot currently connect to anything, so I need to find another way to prepare the nerve route.
reaction: I am unsure why the direct connection did not work.
reason: Inspecting the balance nerves should reveal what they can connect to now.
expectation: The compatibility list should show how to advance the incoming signal route.

effect: The balance nerves joined the eye and posture routes, completing the signal pathway. The body and balance organs still need to be brought into the response.
reaction: The compatibility hint clarified a connection I had missed.
reason: The response routes run through the brain and spinal cord to muscles, so connecting them to the body seems like the next step. I am guessing about the required order.
expectation: The body should gain the nerve routes for responding to balance signals.

alternatives.reason: I could check its available partners before trying the connection.

effect: The body now has the response routes, but the balance sensors remain unconnected.
reaction: The pale spaces make the remaining connection clear.
reason: The balance organs contain both sensor types and fit the unconnected spaces beside the ears.
expectation: The sensors should connect to the body's balance routes, allowing responses to head movement.

effect: Connecting the balance organs completed the body model and showed how balance signals help stabilize vision and posture, alongside information from vision, muscles and joints.
reaction: The eyes turning opposite the head was a satisfying, understandable result.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the balance organs to the body was most worthwhile because it showed what the sensors actually help the body do.

leastWorthwhile.text: Trying to connect the balance organs directly to the nerves was confusing: the attempt gave no explanation of what had to happen first.

surprise.text: I expected the turning sensors to connect directly to nerves, but the feedback joined the two sensor types first.

arbitrary.text: Having to connect the nerve routes to the body before adding the balance organs felt like an unexplained ordering requirement, even though the finished pathway made sense.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: seeing separate sensors become a system that keeps the eyes steady was interesting, though I would hope future prerequisites are clearer.
